title: Exploring Applications of ChatGPT to English Language Teaching: Opportunities, Challenges, and Recommendations
extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT might be used in English Language Teaching (ELT), with a particular focus on balancing pedagogical opportunities against risks such as academic integrity concerns, misinformation, bias, privacy, and overreliance on AI. The authors situate the discussion in the early period of public adoption of ChatGPT and aim to synthesize emerging thinking while also reflecting on their own classroom experimentation in university ELT settings.

The paper combines a narrative review of emerging literature with practice-based classroom examples from the authors’ university. They describe two in-class ChatGPT-supported lessons: one in an undergraduate public speaking course and one in a graduate academic listening and speaking course for international students in a pathways program. In the public speaking lesson, student groups crafted prompts, received ChatGPT-generated debate constructives, analyzed them for ethos/pathos/logos, then revised them using research and personal examples before mock debates. In the graduate course, students compared ChatGPT output on presentation skills with prior knowledge using Venn diagrams. The implementation was explicitly human-in-the-loop, with instructor oversight of prompts and emphasis on critical evaluation of AI output rather than acceptance of responses at face value.

The studied population consisted of undergraduate and graduate international students at Northeastern University in the United States, and the context was authentic in-class higher education instruction rather than a laboratory task. Data reported include classroom observations and short student reflections/surveys capturing attitudes toward ChatGPT. Students were generally engaged and curious, but also skeptical: they valued ChatGPT as a support tool and idea generator, yet frequently questioned its accuracy, depth, and ability to replace human instruction.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can be useful in ELT when used cautiously to stimulate interaction, comparison, retrieval practice, and critical thinking, but should not replace teachers or students’ own intellectual work. The authors recommend collaborative experimentation among educators, explicit reflection with students about responsible AI use, and redesign of learning activities and assessments to emphasize process, creativity, evaluation, and human judgment. Overall, the article is better understood as an exploratory, practice-oriented contribution than as a rigorous causal evaluation of learning effects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed descriptive/practice-oriented article with limited classroom-based qualitative evidence (observations and student quotes) but no formal experimental or quasi-experimental design, no clear sample reporting, and no validated outcome measures. It provides some authentic implementation detail, but credibility is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising but unclear impacts on engagement and critical reflection, with mixed student perceptions and no reported effect sizes. Because impacts are anecdotal and not rigorously estimated, the overall impact remains modest/uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT in university ELT speaking/presentation classes for in-class prompt-based idea generation, debate constructive generation, and comparison of AI output with students' own knowledge; not focused on draft-specific writing feedback.

Discusses ChatGPT as a language-learning and writing-support tool in ELT, including possible grammar correction and writing feedback affordances, but these uses are described conceptually rather than empirically tested in this study.

finding.finding_summary: In the authors' classroom implementations, students appeared more talkative, enthusiastic, and engaged when ChatGPT was used during in-class activities. Evidence is based on instructor observations and illustrative student quotations from short post-activity reflections/surveys rather than a formal comparative design; no effect sizes or validated scales were reported.
finding.measure: Instructor observations; short written reflections/electronic survey comments about engagement, motivation, and attitudes toward ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT use supported critical comparison of AI output with students' own ideas and stimulated discussion about accuracy, limitations, and responsible use, suggesting benefits for critical thinking and evaluation. At the same time, some students felt ChatGPT offered superficial or shortcut-like support that did not teach them how to improve, indicating concerns about overreliance and limited depth. No standardized critical-thinking measures or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student quotations and instructor reflections on critical analysis of ChatGPT output, evaluation of accuracy, and perceived learning value

finding.finding_summary: The classroom activities targeted persuasive speaking, listening, and presentation skills in undergraduate and graduate ELT courses, and the authors qualitatively describe ChatGPT as a useful starting point for discussion and revision of debate constructives and presentation-skill concepts. However, the paper provides no direct pre/post achievement data on speaking or listening gains, and some students questioned whether the tool meaningfully improved learning.
finding.measure: Course-embedded activities in public speaking and academic listening/speaking; student perceptions of usefulness for learning

finding.finding_summary: A major substantive focus of the paper is institutional and classroom-level policy implications: the authors argue for responsible-use policies, collaboration, professional development, and negotiated guidance rather than bans. These are recommendations grounded in literature review and local experimentation, not causal evidence of institutional effects.
finding.measure: Author analysis and recommendations regarding policy, governance, responsible-use guidance, and professional learning
